# Brindle 3.2 documentation

Brindle is an embeddable message-queue library for Go and Rust services.

## Ordering

Messages are delivered in the order they were published within one queue. The guarantee holds per queue, across all
consumers of that queue, as long as the queue has a single writer.

## Flow control

Each consumer may hold at most 10,000 unacknowledged messages. When a consumer falls further behind, Brindle drops
the oldest unacknowledged message to make room for the new one. The drop is not reported to the publisher or the
consumer; the only trace is the counter `brindle_dropped_total`. Raise `max_unacked` (up to 50,000) or add consumers
if a drop is not acceptable.

## Persistence

Queues are kept in memory and written to a write-ahead log every 200 ms by default (`wal_interval`).

# Quarrel 1.4 reference

Quarrel is a partitioned message-queue library.

## Delivery

Delivery is at least once. A message that is not acknowledged within `ack_timeout` (30 s by default) is delivered
again, so consumers must be idempotent.

## Ordering

Order is kept within a partition only. A queue is split into 64 partitions by default, and messages of one queue in
different partitions may be delivered in any order. Pin a key to a partition (`partition_key`) to keep the order of
the messages that share it.

## Back-pressure

A publisher blocks when the partition buffer is full; no message is dropped.

# "Quarrel is 3x faster than Brindle" — Quarrel Inc. engineering blog

We published 10 million 1 KB messages through Quarrel 1.4 and Brindle 3.2 on our own c7-metal test rig.
Quarrel reached 3.1 million messages per second, Brindle 1.0 million.

Method notes: one run per library, default settings, the Brindle WAL interval left at its default. The rig and the
harness are not public.

final.result:
**Quarrel fits better.** It only meets your ordering requirement if you configure it for that.

**Brindle 3.2 doesn't meet "never lose messages silently."**
- Ordering is good. Messages stay in order per queue, as long as each queue has a single writer.
- Loss is the problem. If a consumer has more than `max_unacked` unacknowledged messages (10,000 by default, 50,000 at most), Brindle drops the oldest one. Neither the publisher nor the consumer is told. The only sign is the `brindle_dropped_total` counter.
- Queues live in memory and are written to the log every 200 ms, so a crash can also lose up to about 200 ms of messages.

**Quarrel 1.4 meets the no-loss requirement.**
- When a buffer is full, the publisher waits instead of a message being dropped.
- Delivery is at least once, so a message can arrive twice. Your consumers need to handle duplicates safely.
- Ordering is the catch. Order is only kept within a partition, and each queue is split into 64 partitions by default. To get strict order across a whole queue, use one partition per queue, or give all of a queue's messages the same `partition_key`. Either way you lose the throughput the partitions would give you.

**Ignore these two sources:**
- The "3x faster" blog post is Quarrel's own benchmark: one run, default settings, and a test setup nobody else can check. Also, it measured Quarrel with 64 partitions, which isn't the setup you'd run. Benchmark your own configuration.
- The forum thread is one anonymous claim, and the poster admits they have no numbers. Quarrel's own docs contradict their "it's ordered" claim.

I saved the key facts from the Brindle and Quarrel docs to the research shelf in memory.
